transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-09-10 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~68 minutes | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (SE), Darren (Infra), Maya (Nebula CTO), Raj (ML), Lin (Platform), Evan (Product), Karen (Procurement)
---
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick agenda — Priya will run through the constrained decoding / JSON-mode perf characteristics, then Darren will touch on VPC/on-prem considerations, and we'll leave time for Q&A and next steps.
[00:14] Maya: Great, thanks Alex. I appreciate focusing on function chaining — that's the main reason we're talking, our pipeline chains a few tool calls and we need strict JSON outputs to avoid extra validation.
[00:24] Priya: Cool. I'll start with a quick primer. When we talk about strict JSON mode we mean run-time constrained decoding: the model is constrained to only emit tokens consistent with a JSON grammar/schema during generation. That avoids post-hoc parsing errors but it does add search space constraints which can increase per-token compute and latency.
[00:42] Raj: Is this the same as the "schema-constrained decoding" that people do with regex or grammar-based masks?
[00:48] Priya: Yes similar idea, but at the runtime level we implement token-level masks and lookahead logic inside the beam/greedy decode. That gives more deterministic outputs for tool calling so you don't have to run heuristics client-side.
[01:02] Alex: Quick callout — in our internal checks on a 8-A100 node we saw anywhere from +4% to +32% latency depending on prompt length and the strictness of schema. Short single-field JSONs were close to +5%, deeply nested schemas with many constraints hit the high end.
[01:18] Lin: That range is big. What's driving the 32% case?
[01:22] Priya: Two big factors: (1) token-level lookahead/validation increases the per-token candidate scoring work — effectively we prune invalid tokens but we also do extra checks to update the valid-token set. (2) When you have function chaining we frequently flush or switch contexts which causes KV cache misses — more on that in a bit.
[01:38] Raj: Can you explain the KV cache miss interaction? I thought KV cache persists across tokens to speed up autoregressives.
[01:44] Priya: Right — normally the KV cache holds past key/values for the current ongoing prompt so subsequent tokens are cheap. But for tool chaining you often end a model call, run an external tool, then start a fresh assistant call with some of the previous context reconstructed. If that reconstruction isn't a perfect prefix or if you switch to a slightly different model variant (e.g., quantized int8), the runtime may not be able to reuse the cache and needs to re-encode which costs latency.
[02:06] Darren: Also worth noting in Dedicated/On-prem modes, the NIC and kernel selection affect how quickly KV blocks move between GPUs or sockets. If you have slow interconnects or heterogenous GPUs we see added latency during context switching.
[02:18] Maya: Nebula is considering a VPC on-prem setup with 2xH100s per node and 200Gbps IB. Will that minimize the cache miss pain?
[02:26] Darren: It'll help, yes. 200Gb IB is good. Two things: make sure your CPU to GPU PCI lanes aren't saturated during memory copies, and keep the kernel/backends consistent — mixing a quantized inference runtime on one node and a different build on another can force re-compiles or disable some fused kernels.
[02:42] Lin: On the quantization note — what's your guidance for int8 vs bf16 with strict JSON? We care about determinism and token stability.
[02:50] Priya: Int8 quant improves throughput and reduces memory but sometimes increases token-level distribution jitter — for constrained decoding that can show up as more candidate ties and slight differences in token ordering. For strict schema outputs you usually want a mix: keep the head of the model bf16 for stability for the first N layers and int8 quant the rest, or use a QAT-profile we ship. That gets you most of the perf wins without large changes in determinism.
[03:16] Raj: Does Redwood provide those mixed quant profiles or is it something we run on-prem?
[03:20] Priya: We provide recommended quant profiles for each model and hardware profile. For Private deployments we can prebuild the optimized kernels together with your infra. That's where Darren's checklist helps.
[03:28] Evan: Back to function chaining overhead — concretely, how much extra latency do we pay per intermediate tool call? We chain 3 calls in the worst case.
[03:34] Alex: In our numbers, a simple tool call round trip with a small payload (think 10 tokens returned) adds 40-120ms depending on whether the runtime can reuse the KV cache. If you can't reuse the cache it's more like 150-300ms because of re-encoding/rehydration. So three sequential calls can add up and the strict JSON encoding on each call pushes each of those by that +4-32% factor.
[03:56] Priya: Another leaky bucket is batching: to get throughput we batch requests, but batching increases tail latency. For JSON strictness we recommend keeping the headroom for latency SLOs by setting max batch delay smaller when you know calls need constrained decoding. Also consider auto-join: group similar schema calls together to improve mask reuse across the batch.
[04:16] Raj: "Mask reuse across the batch" — explain?
[04:18] Priya: If multiple requests in a batch share the same JSON schema, the runtime can compute the valid-token sets once and amortize that work across the batch. If every request has a different schema you do the expensive mask computations per request and it scales poorly. So we recommend schema bucketing before batching.
[04:33] Lin: Does Redwood's runtime do schema bucketing automatically or do we need to add logic on client side?
[04:37] Priya: We do both. On Hosted/Dedicated we have hooks that try to bucket by schema fingerprint. For Private you can enable the same behavior or do client-side routing if you prefer stricter control.
[04:46] Maya: What about streaming vs non-streaming? We need some outputs to start streaming while still enforcing JSON schema. Is that supported?
[04:53] Priya: Streaming with strict JSON is tricky because you might stream partial tokens that later become impossible given a later token or mask update. Our recommendation is to stream only after a minimal validation prefix is satisfied, or stream at field-level granularity — e.g., don't stream until the opening brace and key are committed. That reduces the complexity and preserves determinism.
[05:13] Raj: Any hacks like post-generate correction? Could we run unconstrained generation and then have a lightweight parser that fixes up JSON instead of constrained decoding?
[05:20] Priya: That's a valid pattern. It's often cheaper: unconstrained generation plus a deterministic post-processor that corrects known error classes can be lower-latency than constrained decoding for moderately complex schemas. But it trades off the guarantee — you could still get semantically invalid outputs that are hard to repair. If your webhook/toolchain cannot tolerate failures, constrained decoding is safer.
[05:40] Alex: We actually ran an internal benchmark: for 25-field flat JSONs unconstrained + parser was ~12% faster p50 than constrained decode but had a ~3% failure rate where repairs weren't trivial. For critical paths that failure rate might be unacceptable.
[05:54] Lin: For the repair approach, does Redwood provide any parsing helpers or validators?
[05:58] Priya: We provide client-side libraries to do schema validation and smart corrections — heuristics are open-source. But note that those are best-effort.
[06:06] Maya: Switching gears — can you speak to model fallbacks? We want to prioritize latency but also have fallback to cheaper model if primary is saturated. How does strict JSON move across models?
[06:16] Priya: Great question. If you fallback to a cheaper model the constrained-decoder mask may still be applied but the token distribution will change so you might see more rejections or longer generation times for certain constructs. We recommend a staged fallback: first try model variant with same tokenizer and quant profile, then a cheaper one. Redwood runtime supports cross-model mask compatibility checks and can abort fallback if schema satisfaction probability is too low.
[06:40] Raj: You mentioned tokenizers — are there tokenizer compatibility pitfalls we should worry about?
[06:44] Priya: Yes — especially with byte-level BPE differences across model families. JSON tokens like quotes, braces can token-split differently which changes the mask effect. We recommend using models with stable tokenization for strict schema workloads.
[06:57] Darren: On infra: Latency is not only model infer time. For on-prem/VPC ensure you have: consistent runtime builds, pinned CUDA/cuDNN/Kernel combos, consistent quant libraries, and a NIC configuration that minimizes copy latency. We'll provide a checklist with exact kernel versions we've validated.
[07:15] Maya: Would we need to run a dedicated fleet for this pipeline versus mixing with general workloads?
[07:19] Darren: If your SLOs are strict (e.g., p95 < 300ms) I'd recommend a dedicated pool. Mixing workloads increases variance and can lead to KV eviction if memory pressure occurs. Dedicated capacity also lets you pin model versions and quant kernels.
[07:33] Evan: Pricing question — how should we think about cost for dedicated nodes when constrained decoding reduces throughput?
[07:39] Alex: Practically it's about two levers: (1) throughput per GPU — constrained decoding reduces tokens/sec, (2) batching behavior — smaller batches to hit latency targets reduce utilization. We'll work up an estimate for your expected QPS and acceptable p95 to size the dedicated pool.
[07:55] Lin: On the benchmarking that Priya will run, can we get p50/p95/p99 and token-cost breakdowns? Also breakdown by time spent in mask calc vs kernel infer vs KV rehydrate?
[08:05] Priya: Yes, we'll provide a breakdown. Our profiler emits token-level timings and splits out mask computation, attention/kernels, KV I/O, and host-to-device copies. For private runs we'll share a flamegraph and per-stage numbers.
[08:18] Raj: A nit — in past calls we've seen Fireflies transcripts mess up SSO vs SAML acronyms — so when you send the checklist please include the SAML SSO flow for Nebula's IdP.
[08:29] Alex: Noted. We'll include auth flows in the security doc.
[08:33] [08:33] Karen (procurement): Quick procurement question — NRE for on-prem build and extended support costs?
[08:39] Alex: We'll include a two-part quote: (A) dedicated capacity monthly commit, (B) one-time NRE for integration and kernel tuning. We'll surface the NRE separately.
[08:49] [08:49] Maya: Ok, some follow-ups from my side — we need to ensure logs/audit trail for each tool invocation and tie outputs back to request ids. Does Redwood capture that?
[08:58] Priya: Yes. Redwood Console captures per-request metadata, per-token costs, and you can turn on rich audit logs for Private deployments which include function-call traces. We'll show an example in the next demo.
[09:09] Raj: Could you share the rough microbenchmark methodology so we can reproduce locally?
[09:13] Priya: Sure: we'll share a repo. High level: 1) run baseline unconstrained decode for prompt set at batch sizes [1,4,8], 2) run constrained JSON mode with same batches, 3) vary cache reuse (warm/cold), 4) run with quant profiles (bf16, int8, mixed), 5) collect per-token timings and parse success rates. We'll include scripts to simulate tool chaining.
[09:34] Lin: For cold cache tests — are you going to simulate re-encode or real external-tool latency?
[09:38] Priya: Both. We'll do synthetic KV flushes to measure re-encode costs and also a full roundtrip including a 50-200ms mock tool to show end-to-end impact.
[09:46] Evan: On the mock tool latencies — those will dominate real world more often than the constrained decode cost, correct?
[09:51] Priya: Right, if your tool calls are 200-400ms then that's the primary contributor. Where strict JSON costs bite is when the tool payload is tiny and you're sensitive to per-token jitter.
[10:02] [10:02] Maya: Anything else we should be mindful of from a data/security standpoint for on-prem?
[10:07] Darren: KMS integrations, HSM for key storage, audit log retention, and network segmentation. We'll share the firewall port list and a hardened container image. Also, be aware of kernel/user namespace constraints if you use SGX-type enclaves — that can affect performance.
[10:22] Raj: One more technical question — does constrained decoding prevent certain degenerate loops or token repetition issues?
[10:27] Priya: It can help by forbidding tokens that violate grammar, but it won't stop semantic loops unless the grammar captures that. For repetition the runtime still uses typical repetition penalties; constrained masks reduce syntactically invalid loops though.
[10:40] Alex: We're about halfway through so maybe we fast-forward to a couple concrete examples we've seen in the wild. Priya — you had that example with a 6-field nested schema plus two tool calls where p95 jumped a lot?
[10:49] Priya: Yes. Example: a generate->validate->augment chain where each step emits a nested JSON. In the live test we saw p95 double from ~280ms to ~560ms when we added strict JSON on each step, largely due to repeated KV re-encodes and small-batch inefficiencies. Once we bucketed the calls by schema and precomputed masks those numbers dropped to ~320ms. The key is avoiding repeated cold rehydrates and maximizing mask reuse.
[11:15] Lin: Precompute masks — do you mean at compile time?
[11:18] Priya: We can precompute token-valid sets for static schemas and cache them on the runtime. For dynamic schemas we can do partial precompute or incremental mask updates.
[11:27] Raj: Is mask storage heavy? If we precompute for 100 schemas does it blow up memory?
[11:32] Priya: Typically it's small compared to KV cache. Masks are boolean maps per vocab token per position window but we compress them and only store diffs for similar schemas. In practice storing a few thousand schema masks is feasible.
[11:45] Maya: Ok good. We're close on time — quick recap and who's doing what?
[11:50] Alex: Recap: Redwood to run microbenchmarks; share perf breakdowns and VPC/on-prem checklist + NRE estimate. Nebula to send pilot prompts and schema. We'll schedule follow-up run.
[12:02] Priya: I'll also include a section with recommended batching configs: target p95 thresholds and how to set max_batch_delay and schema-bucketing rules.
[12:11] Lin: One last ask — can we see a side-by-side of constrained vs parse-correct/error rates?
[12:16] Priya: Yes, that'll be part of the microbenchmark artifact.
[12:20] Maya: Thanks, this was useful.
[12:22] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts and a calendar invite for the 9/22 on-prem slot.
